text:
kevin: proposing we land on a clear ownership model for north-south egress in Private deployments. i sketched three options, want quick reactions before i turn into an RFC.

kevin: Option A — Platform-centralized gateway (shared pool). platform owns and scales a central egress fleet per-region, all customer control-plane traffic hairpins out through this. cheaper, easier to operate, single audit stream. downsides: cross-tenant surface, noisy neighbors, harder per-tenant flow logs.

anya: 👍 cheaper sounds good for PLG customers. but enterprise will push back on shared IPs / audit. also curious about SNAT preservation for IP allowlists.

kevin: good call. SNAT is a pain. central pool means we SNAT with platform-owned addresses unless we prefix customer routes. preserving source IP is tricky without per-tenant NGW or using proxy protocol.

sasha: Option B — Platform-owned per-customer egress (dedicated gateway per tenant). isolates logs & IPs, easier compliance, can map dedicated public IPs, better mitigation for noisy neighbors. cons: higher infra cost, more warm standby capacity, more routing complexity.

matt: Option C — Customer-owned egress (delegate to customer VPC NAT / appliance). simplest for platform: we route control-plane outbound to customer internet via peering/export routes and let them manage. pros: best for compliance; cons: we lose unified observability, more ops support, and we can't reliably enforce SNI/TLS inspection for fallback.

anya: For private control plane, we also need to think about path for agent check-ins and webhooks. customers will often require egress to be blocked except specific IPs. if central pool changes IPs during autoscale that breaks allowlists.

kevin: here's a quick matrix I wrote down:
- Cost: A < C < B
- Isolation/compliance: B > C > A
- Operational complexity: A < C < B
- Observability & tracing: B >= A > C

sasha: question: can we do hybrid? default to A for PLG & small customers, offer B as enterprise paid option, and support C as a last resort? That seems obvious but we need migration story.

kevin: exactly, hybrid is our likely product outcome. but we need concrete constraints: e.g., for B we should support per-tenant pools with automated cold-start, and an assignment API so SRE doesn't hand-provision. also autoscaler must be able to scale to 100s of tenants.

matt: about per-tenant pools—two implementation patterns: 1) per-tenant NAT gateways in our VPCs (k8s service per-tenant) or 2) shared host pool with eBPF-based per-tenant SNAT mapping. pattern 2 reduces infra but more complex.

anya: eBPF mapping idea sounds cool but then kernel compatibility across customers (on-prem vs cloud) will be a support headache. prefer per-tenant K8s service for first cut.

kevin: Agreed. MVP B: provision per-tenant k8s namespace + egress gateway Deployment + NodePort/public EIP. automation via terraform module + operator. sample route table snippet we might apply on customer's route table for delegated flows:```
resource "aws_route" "to_egress" {
  route_table_id = var.customer_rt
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.egress.id
}
```

sasha: For central A, we should guarantee IP stability SLA (sticky pools) and publish a CIDR per-region with a retention policy so customers can allowlist. also need rate limiting & per-tenant rate shaping to avoid noisy neighbor impact.

infra-bot: deploy-bot: created issue #3421 (egress-gateway-ownership-modes) linking RFC skeleton https://redwood.internal/r/3421

matt: rollout plan idea: 1) implement central A in regions we already own (low effort), 2) implement automation for B (per-tenant provisioning) behind feature flag, 3) add console controls + billing tag for B customers, 4) support C via docs + egress validation tests.

anya: operational alerts: for B we need per-tenant capacity metrics and a per-tenant cost dashboard. also must think about DDoS mitigation if we expose per-tenant IPs.

kevin: security note: TLS termination must remain in customer agent when possible. for central A, we should avoid terminating TLS for customer traffic — do TCP passthrough or mTLS to the controlplane. For things we must inspect (e.g., health callbacks), we should have clear customer opt-in.

sasha: i raised a concern about hairpin NAT for on-prem private endpoints. if control-plane is in platform and data plane in customer VPC, routing must avoid hairpin loops. we should ensure agents dial out (outbound TLS) instead of inbound connections wherever possible.

matt: agree, outbound-only agent model reduces firewall friction. but some customers insist on peering and private links; in those cases we need to document tradeoffs and fallback behavior.

kevin: next steps: i'll convert this into a short RFC. ask infra to prototype per-tenant k8s egress with operator — matt can own spike. sasha can draft console UI changes for allocation/flags. anya can capture enterprise requirements for IP stability and audit.

anya: i'll collect 3 enterprise customers' allowlist constraints and share.

matt: i'll start the spike this week, will post logs and perf numbers.

kevin: thanks all. if nobody objects within 48h I'll open RFC and tag architecture. :thumbsup:
